transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-28
Time: 16:00 PST
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Luis Ortega (Redwood SE), Sasha Patel (Elmwood Head of ML), Dr. Aaron Blake (Elmwood CTO), Jenna Morris (Elmwood Security)

Summary (auto): Short demo walkthrough of Redwood rate limiting, org/project key model, and console controls. Discussed enforcement semantics, tenant isolation, RBAC, and next steps for a short POC. Some transcription errors present.

Transcript:
00:00 Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, um we're excited to walk through how Redwood handles rate limits and org/project keys for multi-tenant setups.
00:08 Sasha: thanks, yes excited. quick context — we run inference for a few clinical tools, multi-tenant, and latency matters. looking to understand controls and separation between teams.
00:18 Luis: great, i'll share my screen — oh small note, you might see my terminal fonts huge, sorry. so first slide is the high-level: orgs map to billing/administration, projects are per-application keys and quotas.
00:33 Dr. Aaron: so projects are like API keys scoped to a product?
00:36 Luis: yeah exactly, project keys are the per-app credential you embed, org keys are the admin/top-level controls. you can set quotas and rate limits at both levels.
00:48 Maya: one of the common questions is 'what happens when a project exceeds quota, does it impact other projects in the same org?' quick answer is no, isolation by default, we can also define shared pool behavior.
01:05 Jenna: and from security side how are keys rotated and stored? do you support customer-managed KMS?
01:12 Luis: yes we integrate with KMS/HSM, keys in transit TLS 1.2+, at rest encrypted. key rotation is supported via the console or API, and you can require hardware-backed. the console shows key metadata and last-rotated. (mumbled) sorry transcription says KMS as K-M-S sometimes KMS spelled K M S.
01:32 Sasha: good. also want to understand rate limit shapes — burst vs sustained?
01:36 Luis: we have token-based quotas and request-per-second limits. burst windows and token buckets, and you can set hard or soft limits. soft triggers can route to a degraded model or queue.
01:49 Maya: demonstration time — we'll show the console, then an API demo with a project key, and then an Optimize suggestion for batching.
01:55 [screen shares — console shows org settings]
02:12 Luis: so here's the org dashboard, top-left you can see org-wide quota (monthly tokens), then a project list. I'm clicking into 'elmwood-dev' project.
02:28 Luis: note the project has a per-minute RPS limit and per-month token quota. we also have per-route limits, so you could throttle generation endpoints separately from embeddings.
02:44 Sasha: embeddings are heavy for us, so that'll be key. can we set separate budgets per team?
02:49 Luis: yes, projects map to teams. you can attach billing codes, and create sub-projects if you want finer granularity.
03:03 Dr. Aaron: what about graceful degradation — if they hit the limit, do you return 429s or is there an automatic fallback?
03:09 Luis: configurable. by default you get 429 with X-RateLimit headers, but you can configure a fallback policy — route to a smaller model variant or to cached responses, or route to a queue that will smooth spikes. we can demo that in POC.
03:25 Maya: one thing to highlight — org-level holds administrative rights, so only org admins can change quotas or generate new project keys. project-level API keys cannot change org settings.
03:36 Jenna: for compliance we need audit logs. are quota changes logged?
03:40 Luis: yes all admin changes are in audit logs with actor, timestamp, and IP. logs can be exported to S3 and streamed to customer SIEM.
03:50 Sasha: how do you handle shared resources — say two projects suddenly spike, do we have a fair-share algorithm?
03:56 Luis: we have multiple policies — strict per-project isolation (hard limits), shared-burst pool (you allocate a burst pool for the org and projects pull from it), and priority weighted fairness for critical projects.
04:18 Maya: quick API demo, i'll paste a curl hitting the generation endpoint with a project key. note: this key is scoped to project and has the per-minute rate encoded in headers we return.
04:34 Maya: curl -H \"Authorization: Bearer proj_key_xxx\" https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate -d '{\"prompt\":\"summarize patient note\"}' (transcript artefact: quotes and backslashes may be mis-captured)
04:48 Speaker 1: hmm can you show the response headers?
04:50 Luis: yes here, X-RateLimit-Limit: 60, X-RateLimit-Remaining: 59, X-RateLimit-Reset: 16 (seconds). also X-Token-Quota etc.
05:05 Sasha: those header names are helpful. do SDKs surface these?
05:08 Luis: SDKs expose them on the response object and we have helpers to back off and retry with jitter.
05:16 Dr. Aaron: curious about multi-tenant data isolation — if two projects share a model instance, is KV cache shared?
05:23 Luis: by default KV cache is isolated per-project. we can configure shared caching for very low-latency cross-project use-cases but by default isolation is the safe path.
05:38 Sasha: what about billing reconciliation when usage flows between projects?
05:42 Maya: the billing is tied to projects, and org-level billing will show aggregated and per-project breakdowns. exports available daily.
05:50 Jenna: any PII concerns in logs? we need tokens scrubbed and redactions.
05:54 Luis: logs can be redacted at ingestion, and we have a PII scrubber pipeline; you can opt into no-text-logging at the org level which turns off full transcript logging.
06:08 Maya: now Optimize — we'll run the model recommendation tool. it looks at your traffic, suggests batching settings, quantization and cache TTLs.
06:18 Luis: for example for your embeddings heavy workload it will suggest batching 8-16 with a 50ms queue threshold, and suggest a mid-quantized variant for large-batch throughput to save cost.
06:33 Sasha: can Optimize suggest thresholds that obey our latency SLOs?
06:36 Luis: yes you feed SLO targets and Optimize will recommend the trade-off curve — e.g., 10% higher p95 for 30% lower $/token.
06:48 Dr. Aaron: great. any guard rails to prevent Optimize from changing production config automatically?
06:52 Maya: Optimize only suggests; autopilot changes are opt-in and require org admin approval and can be rolled back.
07:02 Jenna: security question — does Optimize need access to raw request content to recommend?
07:06 Luis: it can operate on aggregated telemetry and token counts, but for better suggestions you can allow sampled prompt traces. sampling rates are configurable and traces are redacted unless you opt-in for full text.
07:18 Sasha: timeline — we're hoping to run a two-week POC in early Jan, run our typical 24-hour peak and some long tail tests. is that doable?
07:26 Maya: yes we can provision a trial org and project keys, run a benchmark with your scripts. Luis will work with you to make the load profile.
07:34 Luis: i'll put together a benchmark checklist — endpoints, concurrency, sample prompts, and we'll collect token breakdowns and latency hist.
07:42 Dr. Aaron: any SLAs for Dedicated vs Hosted?
07:45 Maya: Hosted has best-effort and SLOs in console; Dedicated comes with SLA and reserved GPU pools and different pricing. we'll send the SLA doc.
07:56 Sasha: pricing note — curious about overage charging and negotiated caps.
07:59 Maya: we'll include pricing matrix and recommended commitment levels.
08:06 [brief cross-talk — someone unmuted]
08:12 Luis: demo wrap-up — quick recap: projects are per-app keys and quotas, orgs are admin/billing and can set org-wide pools and policies, keys integrate with KMS, audit logs available, Optimize suggests batching and quantization.
08:25 Maya: next steps we captured: trial org, send docs, schedule POC run.
08:30 Sasha: sounds good, thanks both.
08:33 Jenna: thanks, appreciate it.
